The Taiga vole (Microtus xanthognathus) is a relatively large-bodied arvicoline rodent inhabiting boreal forests and muskeg habitats of northwestern North America. Gestation in this species proceeds for 22 days [tg = 22 days] when females are maintained at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a duration consistent with the typical interval reported for related voles. Neonates emerge weighing approximately 2.1 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.1 grams], a modest birth mass that is characteristic of altricial microtine rodents. The short gestation period and small litter mass at birth suggest a reproductive strategy oriented toward rapid population turnover, an adaptation to the short, intense growing seasons of high-latitude environments. Litters generally contain between 6 and 13 pups, and under optimal conditions, females achieve a reproductive rate that reflects both relatively large litter sizes and frequent postpartum estrus. Adult males ultimately attain a maximum wet body weight reaching 160 grams [Wwi = 160 grams], making this species one of the largest within the genus Microtus. This considerable body size may confer advantages in thermoregulation and competitive dominance during the brief subarctic summer.

Respirometry trials conducted at a controlled thermal condition of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] have established the basal oxygen consumption rate of the Taiga vole at 98.60 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 98.60 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This elevated metabolic demand likely reflects the species' large body mass relative to other voles, as well as the thermoregulatory costs associated with its northern distribution. Maintaining such a high resting metabolism requires substantial energy intake, which is consistent with the vole's reliance on high-quality forage such as grasses, sedges, and forbs during the active season. The metabolic data further imply that sustained activity at low ambient temperatures would demand a considerable increase above basal rates, potentially limiting the duration of surface activity during harsh winter conditions. These physiological measurements were obtained from adult individuals, providing a reliable baseline for comparative studies among arvicoline rodents and highlighting the species' adaptation to cold environments through elevated endogenous heat production.

The maximum record for longevity in Microtus xanthognathus, based on both field recapture data and captive maintenance, is approximately 1.5 years [am = approximately 1.5 years] at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. When measured in a laboratory setting at a consistent body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], this short lifespan is typical for small mammals with high metabolic rates and a fast pace of life. Such a truncated life history is accompanied by an early and intensive reproductive effort, a common strategy among arvicoline rodents subject to high predation pressure and severe seasonal mortality. Field studies indicate that few individuals survive to a second breeding season, with the majority of the population turning over annually. This high replacement rate is supported by the species' potential for a rapid reproductive output, which compensates for the elevated adult mortality rates characteristic of its dynamic boreal ecosystems.

Sexual maturation in this vole is attained at 290 days after birth [tp = 290 days after birth], a value recorded in captive colonies held at a physiological temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Unlike some congeners that reach breeding condition within a few weeks of birth, Microtus xanthognathus shows a delayed onset of puberty that may relate to the time required to achieve the large adult body size typical of this species. Females typically enter their first estrus during the spring following their birth, synchronizing the initiation of reproduction with the onset of plant growth. Following a successful mating, the offspring remain dependent on maternal milk for only 12 days after birth [tx = 12 days after birth], a remarkably short nursing period given the large body mass of the species at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This abbreviated weaning age (12 days after birth) [tx = 12 days after birth] is facilitated by the high nutritional quality of the vole's milk, which enables rapid neonatal growth at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. The transition to solid food and independence occurs swiftly, allowing females to rapidly initiate subsequent litters within the same breeding season.

Under the thermal conditions characteristic of active physiological processes in this species, maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], individual females can produce an impressive reproductive output. Litter sizes average 8.8 pups per litter [N_R_i = 8.8 pups per litter], and females are capable of delivering approximately two litters per year [F_R_i = approximately two litters per year] when environmental conditions permit. This annual reproductive rate is substantial compared to many other boreal rodents, reflecting the Taiga vole's strategy of producing multiple, moderately large litters to offset high juvenile mortality. The juvenile growth period is brief, with young doubling their birth mass rapidly under the protection of the maternal nest. Predation by mustelids, raptors, and owls exerts strong selective pressure for early independence and high fecundity. By investing heavily in each reproductive opportunity, Microtus xanthognathus maintains stable populations despite the challenges of its short growing season and low primary productivity. The species' remarkable capacity for rapid population growth is a key factor in its success across the northern taiga.
